rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-An‘ām had invited Quraysh to Abraham’s religion, while their innovations and superstitions had no basis in it; God had favoured them with a messenger and warned them through the fate of earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: The basis of this call was that it is Islam which is the religion of Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-A‘rāf is Al-An‘ām’s counterpart: warning dominates here where preaching dominated there, and a charge sheet against Quraysh leads into the histories of earlier nations.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is the counterpart of Sūrah al-An‘ām, the previous sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah also gives Jews a final admonition and closes by recalling the covenant rooted in human nature, before migration and divine punishment follow.
rows.anchor: With the Quraysh, the Jews are also sounded a final admonition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must warn through the Book and convey the truth, while acceptance is not his responsibility; Quraysh are warned by earlier nations’ destruction and coming accountability, where deeds are exposed and weighed.
rows.anchor: He is not responsible to make the accept faith. Only the believers will benefit from this Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s political authority and livelihood were God’s gift, but Satan made them ungrateful; Adam’s story shows Satan’s announced plan to mislead most of humanity, now succeeding with Quraysh.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh are warned that the political authority they enjoy in this land was blessed to them by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By following Satan, Quraysh lost both inner piety and outer clothing, even performing naked circumambulation and falsely treating the practice as ancestral and divinely sanctioned.
rows.anchor: By obeying Satan, they have disrobed themselves of both the inner and outer attire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh have no basis for declaring adornments or wholesome food unlawful; God instead forbids indecency, injustice, rebellion, polytheism, and false attribution, while each nation has an appointed term.
rows.anchor: there is no basis of what they regard to be lawful and unlawful out of their own whims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam’s descendants were instructed to obey messengers: their followers enter Paradise and deniers enter Hell; Paradise’s inhabitants gratefully affirm that the messengers’ promises came true.
rows.anchor: Those who will follow them will go to Paradise and those who will deny them will go to Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise’s inhabitants confirm that God fulfilled His promises, while God’s curse is pronounced on Hell’s companions; watchers in elevated turrets witness fulfilment and rebuke the damned.
rows.anchor: The inhabitants of Paradise will inform the inhabitants of Hell that the promises God made with them were fulfilled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are told that God alone creates and governs the universe, that they should invoke Him in hope and fear and avoid disorder, and that judgement is certain as signs of new life show.
rows.anchor: it is solely God Who creates and runs this universe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shu‘ayb show that God removes nations that spread disorder and reject their messengers.
rows.anchor: They show that God wipes out those nations from the face of the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brief lessons from prior nations warn Quraysh, their successors, to learn from those peoples’ fates; their sealed hearts prevent them from taking heed.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh are warned that they are the successors of these nations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Pharaoh’s history shows that Pharaoh’s schemes could not defeat Moses.
rows.anchor: The anecdote of Moses (sws) and the Pharaoh is mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses account concludes that God destroyed wrongdoers and gave political authority to the oppressed because of their perseverance.
rows.anchor: perseverance. Verses (137-171): A comprehensive comment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel’s history displays God’s repeated kindness and their persistent ingratitude; they still oppose the truth entrusted to them, making this their last chance before lasting humiliation.
rows.anchor: A comprehensive comment is made on all the phases of the history of the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion recalls humanity’s covenant and Israel’s fate, warns Quraysh that idols cannot save them from punishment, and directs the Prophet to be patient, overlook opponents, and remember God.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh are reminded of the covenant drawn from human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added Ṣād joins the abbreviated letters discussed at the start of Al-Baqarah; sūrahs with similar names share topics, and Al-A‘rāf resembles Al-Baqarah despite different periods and audiences.
rows.anchor: there are many aspects in which this sūrah is similar to S ūrah al-Baqarah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers parsing Alif Lām Mīm Ṣu‘ād as an independent sentence with an omitted subject and the next clause with its own omitted subject; connecting the letters to the next verse is also possible, with little semantic difference.
rows.anchor: I have preferred the first option and regard  ۡ ﻟﻴﻚٌٰ"ۡﻛﺘﺐ ﻧﺰل to also have a suppressed inchoative as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for worry means anxiety; the verse was revealed to ease the Prophet’s distress under intense opposition and concern that he was falling short.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has reduced both these burdens.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reassures the Prophet amid Quraysh’s peak hostility and his fear that he is failing to persuade them: God revealed the Book without the Prophet requesting it and will support the mission.
rows.anchor: The God Who has revealed it will provide help and support in this matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the Prophet’s responsibility, the resources it requires, and the strength needed to clear its obstacles, and will provide them so he should be at ease.
rows.anchor: God will provide all these things to him. Hence, he should not worry and rest assured.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s duty is to warn disbelievers and deliver the message; whether Quraysh accept is outside his responsibility.
rows.anchor: His responsibility is to only warn them and deliver the message to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaryah can mean either a city or its inhabitants, so pronouns and verbs may refer alternately to the word or its meaning, a common linguistic usage.
rows.anchor: The word ۡ occurs both for a city as well as for its inhabitants.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaylūlah means taking an afternoon rest, not necessarily sleeping; in hot Arabia people rested in their homes, tents, orchards, and other shelters.
rows.anchor: sleeping is not its essential component.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about believers is grammatically coordinated in meaning with the command to warn but expressed as a noun, marking the fact that believers alone benefit from the reminder.
rows.anchor: it is in the form of a noun instead of a verb.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He supports the reminder’s benefit for God-fearing people by citing Al-Ṭāhā’s opening, which says the Qur’an was not revealed to burden the Prophet but as a reminder.
rows.anchor: It is only a reminder for those who fear God.

rows.speaker: Interpreters
rows.claim: Interpreters generally take the believers as the addressees of the command to follow revelation.
rows.anchor: Interpreters have generally regarded the believers to be the addressees of this verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the general interpretation, context and wording show that Quraysh’s disbelievers are addressed, as the warning to follow revelation follows the Prophet’s reassurance.
rows.anchor: both its context and words evidence that the disbelievers of the Quraysh are its addressees.

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators understand the verse to mean punishment arrives at night or afternoon while people are asleep.
rows.anchor: Some commentators while considering the words “so, Our scourge descended on them suddenly at night or right in the day when they were resting in the afternoon” opine that God’s punishment comes in the afternoon or night when people are sleeping.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the sleeping-time interpretation as contrary to history and the Qur’an, including 6:47 and 7:97-98; punishment may strike quietly at night or loudly in daylight, and only God can protect people.
rows.anchor: the words under discussion do not imply that God’s punishment comes at a time when people are sleeping.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning to Quraysh is that earlier nations were destroyed whenever God willed; survivors confessed guilt too late, and Quraysh will likewise be powerless if they reject revelation.
rows.anchor: However, this confession will be of no use then.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers warn of both worldly destruction for nations rejecting them and the hereafter’s reward or punishment for everyone; the preceding verses warn Quraysh of the first, these verses of the second.
rows.anchor: God’s Messengers warn people of two things: firstly, the punishment that necessarily visits a nation that denies its messenger; secondly, to the reward and punishment that everyone will necessarily face in the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of collective accountability is illustrated by Hell’s inhabitants admitting that a warner came but they rejected him, as described in 67:8-11.
rows.anchor: The accountability of nations has been mentioned in the Qur’ān thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers’ own accountability is illustrated by God asking them what response people gave, as in 5:109.
rows.anchor: The accountability of the messengers is mentioned thus in the Qur’ān:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s complete narration will expose both messengers’ earnest delivery and their addressees’ deliberate denial, leaving no excuse or chance to protest.
rows.anchor: everything will be thoroughly brought to light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgement Day, only truth tilts God’s scales; evil has no weight, and those whose scales incline succeed while the others are doomed.
rows.anchor: The scale of the Almighty on the Day of Judgement will only be tilted by the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes that the Qur’an gives another principle concerning the weight of deeds, beginning a citation about people who think they act well.
rows.anchor: Regarding the weight of deeds, the Qur’ ān has also mentioned another principle:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though God accepted Adam and Eve’s repentance, divine wisdom sent them from Paradise to earth for a contest against Satan and his progeny; Paradise became the reward for those who prevail.
rows.anchor: the contest was the same which Ibl īs had challenged them for; however, its locus was shifted from Paradise to earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “enemies of one another” casts Adam and Iblīs as opposing parties: Satan may lead Adam’s descendants astray, while they can regain Paradise by defeating his designs.
rows.anchor: Adam (sws) and Ibl īs were sent in this world as two disputing parties.

rows.speaker: Christians
rows.claim: The source says Christians regard humans, like Satan, as sent into this world accursed and developed atonement to escape that stigma.
rows.anchor: they think that human beings like Satan were also sent in this world as accursed beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the Christian account: the Qur’an says Adam entered the world already forgiven, where his descendants must prove themselves through resolve and resist Satan.
rows.anchor: Adam (sws) came in this world after being forgiven.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about living, dying, and being raised on earth depicts humanity’s earthly phases before God shows people what they gained or lost and whether they won.
rows.anchor: after they return, they would be informed by God what they gained and lost and if they won or lost.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh claim their vulgar practice comes from their forefathers, treating inheritance as proof of divine sanction.
rows.anchor: this is that it was this way which they had inherited from their forefathers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cardinal principle for assessing divine directives distinguishes them from Satanic innovations.
rows.anchor: the essence and cardinal principle is alluded to which is always kept in consideration about all divine directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The essence of divine directives distinguishes them from Satanic innovations; applying it shows Quraysh’s practices have no connection to God and were falsely attributed to Him.
rows.anchor: none of these things has even the remotest of relationship with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are warned that failure to reform will bring the fate of similar nations.
rows.anchor: they will meet the same fate as that of nations similar to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s covenant promises messengers for guidance: their followers remain safe from Satan’s trials, while deniers enter Hell.
rows.anchor: those who follow them would remain secure from the trials of Satan and those who deny them would be consigned to Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Hell, followers and leaders mutually blame and curse one another; followers accuse their leaders of misguidance, while leaders assign blame to the followers.
rows.anchor: when they will be united in Hell, they will curse one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saved are pictured facing one another without hatred or rebuke, greeting and congratulating one another while praising God and acknowledging the messengers’ favours.
rows.anchor: There will not be the slightest trace of any hate or rebuke.
